strengths: The paper proposes a simple and practically motivated method: retain only frozen/shared linear heads while sharing the feature extractor, then extend this to iterated Q-learning. This is easy to implement and directly targets an important bottleneck in value-based deep RL: target-network memory overhead.

The empirical results are reasonably broad for the specific problem setting, covering online Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm, plus an offline CQL setting. The method consistently improves over target-free baselines and often approaches or exceeds the target-based baseline in AUC.

The paper uses appropriate aggregate evaluation practices for Atari, including IQM and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals over games and seeds, and provides per-game learning curves and hyperparameter details in the appendix.

The analysis section is useful: gradient cosine similarity and effective-rank measurements provide plausible evidence that the method changes target-free learning dynamics toward more stable target-based behavior and improves representation expressivity.
The method has a favorable simplicity-to-benefit ratio, and the memory argument is compelling in settings where the feature extractor dominates parameter count.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The contribution is mainly a recombination of partial target networks/shared features with iterated Q-learning, and the paper would benefit from a sharper positioning against prior multi-head, bootstrapped, ensemble, and target-network compression approaches.

The evaluation is limited to discrete-action Atari-style domains. The paper motivates large networks, high-dimensional inputs, multimodal settings, and memory-constrained scaling, but does not directly evaluate those regimes or continuous-control settings.

The baselines are incomplete for fully supporting the claims. In particular, comparisons to full target-based iterated Q-Networks, ensemble DQN-style methods in the online setting, and stronger target-free regularized methods would clarify whether the gains come from iteration, shared frozen heads, ensembling, or extra output heads.

The memory and training-time claims are not quantified rigorously enough. Parameter-count plots are helpful, but actual GPU memory, activation memory, wall-clock time, and throughput would be more convincing, especially since multiple heads and losses may increase computation and optimizer state.

The method still uses delayed/frozen parameters in the heads, so the framing as target-free or bridging target-free and target-based methods is somewhat slippery. The paper should more carefully define what is meant by target-free versus partial-target-network methods.

There is no theoretical analysis or convergence discussion for the shared-feature iterated setting. Given that shared parameters are updated through all heads while the first head is only partially frozen, the dynamics differ substantially from classical target-network or iterated Q-learning assumptions.

Reproducibility is not yet complete: the paper says the JAX code will be made open source, but availability is not established in the submission, and some implementation details of the IMPALA architecture and offline setup are deferred or summarized only briefly.

strengths: The proposed method is simple and easy to implement: retaining only frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor is a clean way to reduce the parameter overhead of target-network-style methods.
The paper is generally readable and positions the work against relevant target-network, target-free, and iterated Q-learning literature.

The evaluation includes several settings: online Atari with CNN and IMPALA-style architectures, with and without LayerNorm, plus an offline CQL variant. Reporting IQM and bootstrap confidence intervals is appropriate for Atari-style comparisons.
The appendices provide useful implementation details, hyperparameters, game lists, and per-game curves, which help interpret the aggregate results.
weaknesses: The central framing is somewhat overstated: the method is not really target-free, but rather a partial target-network method with shared features and frozen heads. Since the shared feature extractor changes every update, the target is still nonstationary in a way that is not carefully analyzed.

Novelty is limited. The method is mainly a combination of partial target networks/shared representations with previously proposed iterated Q-learning. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish what is conceptually new beyond this combination.

The evidence for the main practical claim, reduced memory footprint, is weak. The paper mostly reports parameter counts, not actual GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, activation memory, or wall-clock throughput. For the motivating use case of scaling network capacity under VRAM constraints, this is a major gap.

The experimental scope is narrower than the claims suggest. Results are on small subsets of Atari games, with 15 or 10 games rather than a full benchmark, and only discrete-action value-based settings. The conclusion gestures toward broad scalability, but the evidence is limited.

Baselines are incomplete. The paper does not compare against stronger or more directly relevant memory-efficient alternatives, such as using the saved target-network memory to enlarge the online network, modern target-free regularized methods, lightweight/low-rank target networks, EMA/Polyak variants, or tuned larger target-based baselines.

Hyperparameter fairness is unclear. The number of heads K is swept for the proposed method, but there is little evidence that baseline learning rates, target update periods, normalization choices, or capacity-matched variants were similarly tuned.

The explanation section is suggestive but not conclusive. Cosine similarity, effective rank, and dormant neuron analyses are correlational and do not establish why the method works or when it should fail.

The paper lacks theoretical support despite making claims about Bellman-iteration chains under shared, continuously changing features. It is unclear whether the iterated interpretation remains valid when all heads share a feature extractor that is updated by all losses.
Offline RL evaluation is limited to one dataset construction and one algorithmic family. This is not enough to support general claims about offline discrete control.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper says the code will be open sourced, but does not appear to provide an available implementation or sufficient detail to fully reproduce all results independently.

strengths: Proposes a simple and appealing middle ground between target-free and target-based value learning: retaining only frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor. The method is easy to understand, cheap in parameters, and plausibly useful for scaling Q-networks under memory constraints.

Connects the method cleanly to iterated Q-learning and shows that learning multiple Bellman iterations in parallel can recover much of the stability/sample-efficiency benefit of target networks without duplicating the whole network.

Empirical evidence is fairly broad for a focused RL paper: online Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures, with and without LayerNorm, plus an offline CQL setting. The paper reports IQM AUC with stratified bootstrap intervals and includes per-game learning curves in the appendix.
The ablations over number of heads are informative, showing both gains and saturation/degradation regimes, and the parameter-count comparisons support the central memory-efficiency motivation.

The diagnostic analyses on gradient similarity, effective rank, and dormant neurons provide useful mechanistic evidence that the method changes learning dynamics in a direction closer to target-based learning.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still limited to discrete-action Atari subsets, not the full ALE suite or continuous-control domains. This narrows the evidence for the paper’s broader claims about scaling reinforcement learning research and applications with large networks.

The method’s novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines shared representations/frozen heads with iterated Q-learning in a natural way. The paper is convincing empirically, but it does not provide theoretical guarantees or a deeper formal account of when shared-feature Bellman chains should be stable.

The main comparisons are mostly against target-based and target-free variants of the same algorithms. Stronger comparisons to recent target-free stabilization methods and memory-efficient target-network alternatives would better establish competitiveness.

The memory-efficiency claim is mainly supported through parameter counts. Actual GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, activation memory, and wall-clock training time are not reported in enough detail, despite being central to the motivation.

The number of heads K is an important new hyperparameter, and the best value varies by architecture/normalization setting. The paper would benefit from clearer guidance or sensitivity analysis beyond the reported choices.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper says the JAX code will be open sourced, but does not provide released code or enough implementation detail to fully verify all engineering choices.

strengths: Simple and appealing idea: keep only stale/frozen linear heads while sharing the feature extractor, giving a practical middle ground between target-free and full target-network value learning.
The method is clearly described and easy to implement, with pseudocode and extensions to DQN, CQL, SAC, and ILQL.

Empirical scope is broad: online Atari, offline Atari, DeepMind Control hard tasks, and a language RL Wordle setting. The paper also reports parameter counts, runtime/FLOPs, per-game curves, and hyperparameters.
Results consistently show improvements over target-free variants, often recovering much of the gap to target-based methods while using substantially fewer Q-network parameters.
The analysis section is useful: gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank, and dormant neuron measurements provide plausible mechanistic evidence beyond raw returns.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: freezing/storing the final layer and adding multiple heads is a lightweight architectural modification built on existing target networks, ensembles, and iterated Q-learning, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The evaluation is convincing relative to target-free baselines, but the main claim of bridging the gap to target-based methods is not uniformly established: some settings only reduce the gap, and several conclusions rely on normalized AUC rather than final performance or task-level statistical tests.

Hyperparameter sensitivity remains a concern. The added K parameter has different optimal values across settings, and the paper does not provide a principled selection rule or enough analysis of robustness to target update rates, architectures, and loss weighting choices.

Comparisons are partly confounded by normalization choices: LayerNorm/BatchNorm are included or excluded differently across target-based, target-free, and iS variants based on observed benefit, which may make some comparisons less clean.

The memory-efficiency framing is narrower than the motivation suggests. The method reduces parameters for target networks, but replay buffers, optimizer state, activations, and multi-head overhead can dominate practical memory; the paper acknowledges this but does not measure full training memory usage.

The method is called target-free in places, but it still relies on stale/frozen heads that function as partial target networks. This positioning could be clearer to avoid overstating the conceptual departure from target-based RL.

There is no theoretical stability or convergence result, even in a simplified setting, so the explanation of why shared changing features plus frozen heads should remain stable is empirical and somewhat speculative.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical issue in deep RL: reducing the memory overhead of target networks while retaining some of their stabilization benefits.
The proposed method is simple and easy to implement: keep frozen/lagged linear heads while sharing the feature extractor, and extend this to multiple heads inspired by iterated Q-learning.
The empirical coverage is broader than many RL papers, spanning online Atari, offline Atari/CQL, continuous control with SAC, and a Wordle/ILQL setting.
The paper reports aggregate metrics with IQM and stratified bootstrap intervals, includes per-task curves and hyperparameter tables, and discusses training time/FLOPs rather than only return.
The ablations over the number of heads and the diagnostic analyses on gradient similarity, target churn, and effective rank are useful for interpreting the method.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main contribution is essentially partial target-network sharing plus multi-head Bellman iteration, both closely related to existing target networks, bootstrapped/multi-head Q-networks, and iterated Q-learning. The paper does not convincingly establish this as a substantial conceptual advance.

The central memory-efficiency claim is overstated. Most figures report parameter counts rather than actual peak GPU memory, and the discussion largely ignores optimizer state, activations, replay buffers, gradients, batch-normalization statistics, and framework overhead. Since training-time VRAM is the motivation, measured peak memory should be a primary result.

The comparisons are not fully clean. In several settings, normalization choices differ across methods, e.g. BatchNorm is used for target-free/iS SAC but not target-based SAC, and LayerNorm is introduced in Atari. This makes it hard to isolate whether improvements come from the proposed target-sharing mechanism, normalization, or their interaction.

The evaluation is broad but not sufficiently definitive. Atari results use 15 games for CNN and only 10 for IMPALA rather than the full benchmark, and the paper provides limited evidence that the selected subset is representative for the claims being made.

The method introduces a new hyperparameter K, and performance is clearly sensitive to K and architecture. The paper does not provide a principled selection rule or account for the tuning cost, yet reports best-looking K values across settings.

The target-free baselines are relatively weak or narrow. The paper claims compatibility with regularization methods, but does not thoroughly compare against the strongest target-free or low-memory alternatives under matched compute, tuning budget, and normalization choices.

There is no theoretical analysis or stability guarantee despite the method using frozen linear heads on non-frozen shared features, which creates nonstationary targets. The intuition is plausible, but the technical support remains empirical and diagnostic.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, such as 'bridging the performance gap' broadly across RL. In several settings the gains are modest, confidence intervals overlap, or the method remains below the target-based baseline.

The paper does not reduce compute or training time in most settings, which weakens the practical resource-efficiency framing. The contribution is mainly parameter-count reduction, not a comprehensive resource-efficiency improvement.

Reproducibility is incomplete for review: code is said to be released upon acceptance, and the supplementary code is not part of the manuscript evidence here. For RL, where implementation details often dominate, this is a meaningful concern.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and appealing alternative between target-free and target-network RL: retain only frozen/shared linear heads while sharing the feature extractor, then extend this with iterated Bellman heads. The method is easy to implement, resource-motivated, and plausibly useful in many value-based RL settings.

The empirical evaluation is broad and stronger than typical for this type of algorithmic RL paper: online Atari with CNN and IMPALA architectures, offline Atari/CQL, DMC/SAC, and Wordle/ILQL. Results consistently show substantial recovery of the target-free performance drop, sometimes matching or exceeding target-based baselines while using many fewer Q-function parameters.

The paper uses appropriate aggregate statistics, including IQM and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, and includes per-task learning curves, hyperparameters, runtime/FLOP analysis, and reproducibility details. This makes the empirical claims relatively transparent.

The analysis section is useful: gradient cosine similarity, target churn, srank, and dormant-neuron measurements provide plausible mechanistic evidence that the shared-head approach both stabilizes targets and improves representations.
The writing is clear, the motivation is well positioned against target networks, target-free regularization, and iterated Q-learning, and the algorithmic contribution is explained cleanly.
weaknesses: The novelty is conceptually moderate rather than groundbreaking: the paper mainly combines partial target-network storage with iterated Q-learning, and the core K=1 idea is simple. The contribution is valuable, but more empirical/engineering than theoretically deep.

The memory-efficiency claim is mostly based on parameter counts. In realistic training, optimizer state, activations, replay buffers, normalization statistics, and framework overhead can dominate memory. Actual peak GPU memory measurements across settings would strengthen the central resource-efficiency argument.

The method introduces K as a new hyperparameter, and the best K varies by setting. The paper reports several K values but does not provide a principled selection rule or a strong sensitivity analysis over target update periods, loss weighting, and architecture size.

Some comparisons are mildly confounded by normalization choices. For example, TF/iS variants use BatchNorm in DMC while the target-based SAC baseline does not, and LayerNorm is important in Atari. These choices are justified empirically, but they complicate attribution of gains solely to the proposed shared-head mechanism.
The evaluation is broad but still uses subsets of Atari games and a single language RL task. Full Atari-57 or additional offline/language benchmarks would make the generality claims more compelling.

There is limited theoretical treatment of stability or approximation error when frozen heads sit on top of changing shared features. The empirical evidence is good, but the paper does not characterize when the approach should fail beyond observed K sensitivity.

strengths: Simple and practically motivated idea: storing/fixing only the final heads while sharing the feature extractor is an appealing middle ground between target-free and full target-network methods.
The empirical evaluation is broad for an RL paper, covering online Atari, offline Atari/CQL, DMC/SAC, Wordle/ILQL, and a streaming setting.
Results are consistently positive versus target-free variants, and often close the gap to or exceed target-based baselines while using substantially fewer Q-function parameters.

The paper reports useful diagnostics and ablations, including gradient cosine similarity, target churn, effective rank, target update period, number of Bellman updates, head width, training time/FLOPs, and per-task curves.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported through detailed hyperparameters, protocol descriptions, seed counts, confidence intervals, and a supplementary code claim.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than major: the method combines partial target sharing with iterated Q-learning, and the core algorithmic change is quite simple relative to prior target-network and multi-head value-learning work.

The central resource-efficiency claim is somewhat overstated. The paper mainly reports parameter counts, while actual peak training memory includes activations, optimizer state, replay buffers, normalization statistics, and framework overhead; measured GPU memory would be more convincing.

The method introduces a new hyperparameter K whose optimal value varies substantially by setting. The recommendation to increase K until performance drops is expensive and weakens the practical simplicity claim.

Comparisons are sometimes confounded by architecture/normalization choices, e.g. BatchNorm used for target-free/iS SAC but not target-based SAC, and LayerNorm choices that are beneficial across methods but make attribution less clean.

The evaluation uses selected Atari subsets and reduced game counts for computational reasons. This is understandable, but full benchmark coverage would be needed to support broad claims about Atari performance.
There is little theoretical analysis of stability or convergence under shared changing features and frozen heads; the explanatory diagnostics are useful but mostly empirical.

Some claimed gains over target-based methods may be fragile, since confidence intervals overlap in several settings and the main normalization of AUC relative to target-based baselines can obscure absolute performance differences.
The continuous-control and language experiments are narrower than the Atari evaluation, so the generality across RL regimes is promising but not fully established.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant practical issue in deep RL: reducing the memory overhead of target networks while retaining much of their stabilizing effect.
The proposed idea is simple and easy to implement: freeze/copy only the final linear head while sharing the feature extractor, and extend this to an iterated multi-head Bellman-update chain.
The empirical scope is broader than many RL papers, covering online Atari, offline Atari/CQL, continuous control with SAC, a Wordle language-RL setting, and a streaming RL variant.

The paper reports robust aggregate metrics with IQM and bootstrap intervals, includes per-game/task curves, and provides useful diagnostics such as gradient similarity, target churn, effective rank, dormant neurons, runtime, FLOPs, and hyperparameter tables.
The method appears to give consistent improvements over target-free baselines in many settings, sometimes recovering much of the target-based performance while using fewer Q-network parameters.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main contribution is a relatively small architectural modification to target networks plus an adaptation of iterated Q-learning; the conceptual advance over target networks, bootstrapped/ensemble heads, and prior iterated Q-network work is incremental.

The central memory-efficiency claim is somewhat overstated. The paper mainly counts Q-network parameters, but in realistic training the replay buffer, optimizer states, activations, normalization statistics, and multi-head forward/backward computation can dominate memory or cost. The method does not generally reduce training time or FLOPs, as the appendix acknowledges.

The evaluation, while broad, is not fully convincing for a top-tier acceptance. Atari uses 15 games or 10 games rather than the full benchmark, streaming uses only 7 games, Wordle is a narrow language-RL proxy, and several conclusions rely on aggregate AUC rather than stronger task-level analysis.

The comparison to target-free baselines is confounded by architectural and algorithmic choices. iS-QN adds multiple heads, changes action selection in discrete control by sampling among heads, and sometimes uses normalization or loss weighting choices whose interaction with the baseline is not exhaustively controlled.

The method introduces a new hyperparameter K, and the best value varies substantially across settings. The recommendation to increase K until performance decreases is computationally expensive and weakens the simplicity claim.

The paper lacks theoretical analysis or stronger evidence about stability. The explanation via target churn, gradient similarity, and effective rank is suggestive but does not establish when sharing features with frozen heads should be stable or beneficial.

Some experiments appear tuned or adapted after observing setting-specific behavior, such as discounting later Bellman-update losses in SAC, while the corresponding design space is not systematically benchmarked.

The significance is somewhat narrow: the method is useful for resource-constrained value-based RL, but the paper does not show a decisive improvement over strong target-based methods, nor does it clearly demonstrate practical deployment benefits beyond parameter-count reduction.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, well-motivated method: keep target-like stability by freezing/copying only the last linear head while sharing the feature extractor, then extend this to multiple heads for iterated Bellman updates. The idea is elegant and practically relevant for memory-constrained deep RL.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an RL methods paper, covering online Atari, offline Atari/CQL, continuous-control SAC on DMC hard tasks, ILQL with GPT-2 on Wordle, and a streaming RL setting. Across these settings, the method consistently improves over target-free baselines and often approaches or exceeds target-based performance with fewer Q-network parameters.

The paper provides useful diagnostics beyond headline returns, including gradient similarity, target churn, effective rank, dormant neurons, parameter counts, runtime/FLOP measurements, and per-task learning curves. These analyses make the mechanism more plausible and help separate memory savings from compute savings.

The positioning is clear: the method is orthogonal to regularization approaches such as MellowMax, LayerNorm/BatchNorm-based stabilization, and mixed precision. The additional experiments support this claim reasonably well.

Reproducibility appears strong: hyperparameters, task selection, evaluation protocol, individual curves, and implementation details are documented, and the authors state that code/dependencies are included in supplementary material.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is mostly architectural/algorithmic rather than theoretically deep. There is no convergence or stability analysis for the shared-feature/frozen-head construction, even though sharing a changing representation with frozen heads is central to the method.

The main benefit is model-parameter memory, not total training resource reduction. The paper acknowledges that runtime and FLOPs are generally similar to target-based methods and that replay buffers, optimizer states, and activations can dominate memory in some regimes. This slightly narrows the practical impact of the headline memory-efficiency claim.

The method introduces a new hyperparameter K, whose optimal value varies substantially across settings. The recommendation to increase K until performance decreases is practical but potentially expensive, especially in RL where tuning costs are high.

Some comparisons are mildly confounded by architecture/normalization choices: LayerNorm or BatchNorm is used differently across variants and domains, and target-based SAC is not given BatchNorm because it hurts performance. These are defensible choices, but they complicate isolating the effect of the proposed head-sharing mechanism.

The Atari evaluation uses subsets of 15 or 10 games rather than a full benchmark suite. The selection is justified and per-game curves are provided, but broader Atari coverage would strengthen claims about generality.

Several gains over target-based methods are empirical and not fully explained; in particular, when iS-QN exceeds target-based baselines, it is not always clear whether the improvement comes from iterated Bellman learning, implicit ensembling/regularization, altered exploration through head sampling, or representation effects.
